{"skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"dotnet-app-delivery","description":"Reusable workflow guidance for scaffolding, building, testing, running, and proving generic .NET applications.","instructions":"Deliver .NET applications with a real scaffold, explicit validation, and durable proof. Use this skill as a .NET specialization of the concrete deliverable delivery skill. It is generic across .NET app domains and project types: console apps, class libraries with tests, web APIs, worker services, ASP.NET Core apps, and Blazor apps.

Start from the project-structure node or step contract. If it names a concrete output directory, treat that directory as the product root even when it is outside the managed workspace. Use `external-target/<drive>/...` aliases for workspace file and dotnet tools when needed. Do not substitute `artifacts/...`, `output/...`, or execution-run evidence folders for the product working directory unless the project structure explicitly says those are the product files.

For greenfield work with an explicit output root and no more specific scaffold contract, split that root into a parent folder and project folder before scaffolding. Example: output root `C:\work\apps\<AppName>` maps to product root `external-target/C/work/apps/<AppName>`; call `workspace_dotnet_new` with `parentDirectory: external-target/C/work/apps` and `name: <AppName>`. When a process scaffold contract names a solution file at the product root, a `src/` app layout, or exact `parentDirectory`/`name` values, that contract overrides this generic shortcut; keep every `workspace_dotnet_new` target inside the grounded product root. Before any scaffold call, check the mapped product root with `workspace_stat_path` or `workspace_list_files` unless the current step already proved the path is absent. If the mapped product root already exists and contains a project or solution, inspect and repair it in place instead of calling `workspace_dotnet_new`, creating a sibling, or writing a managed artifact copy. Then build, test, run, inspect, and summarize files under the mapped product root.

When an exact generated product root is named, resolve the runnable host and test topology from the current delivery contract and grounded project-structure aliases. A root-level host, a `src/` host, a nested test project, or a contract-declared sibling project can all be valid. Treat a sibling, nested project, temporary probe, copied scaffold, or scratch project as a defect only when it is undeclared and substitutes for a declared product or test target. Do not set `BaseOutputPath`, `BaseIntermediateOutputPath`, or `MSBuildProjectExtensionsPath` as an ungrounded path workaround; change output topology only when the contract or a concrete build diagnostic requires it.

Keep generated app projects, support libraries, test projects, scripts, static assets, and evidence helpers inside the roots grounded by the current contract or project structure. For `workspace_dotnet_new`, choose `parentDirectory` and `name` pairs that resolve to the declared topology. Do not impose a universal sibling, `src/`, `tests/`, or `Tests/` layout: use the supplied solution/project aliases and declared project relationships. If no topology is declared for a new small app, choose a conventional contained layout under the product root and record that assumption. Do not create deliverable source, tests, helpers, or assets under managed evidence roots such as `artifacts/`, `output/`, `data/`, or `integration-map/` unless the project structure names one as a product root. If policy denies an ungrounded parent, treat the parent as wrong; do not retry the same parent.

SDK-style default items can include nested project files and outputs. Inspect the declared project graph and the concrete build diagnostic before changing item inclusion or output paths. If a host compiles test sources, copies nested outputs recursively, or reports static-web-asset collisions, repair the responsible project boundary with exclusions or topology changes that fit the existing contract; do not add unrelated packages, impose a different layout pre-emptively, or retry the same command without new evidence.

Keep the requested product domain authoritative. Do not reuse sample app names, old external target paths, remembered source files, or topic-specific acceptance criteria from prior runs unless the current project structure, work brief, or upstream artifact explicitly names them for this run. If policy denies an external-target path, treat the denied path as invalid context for this run; switch to the current grounded product root or current-run artifacts and do not retry that path. Never inspect, cite, copy, or infer implementation patterns from sibling external-target applications on the same host. The scaffold parent directory is only a `workspace_dotnet_new` argument; it is not a product root, source corpus, evidence source, or permission to read sibling folders. Framework patterns must come from loaded skills, official templates, tool descriptions, component-library resources, or current-run artifacts. Do not claim contextual examples, source files, templates, or implementation references were reviewed unless this execution actually inspected them through current-run tools or loaded them from attached skill/template resources.

For greenfield work, create real projects rather than loose source files. Use `workspace_dotnet_new` for approved current SDK templates that match the deliverable type only after confirming the intended root is missing or safe to scaffold. Keep runnable hosts and tests in a clear layout under the product root, and inspect the generated `.csproj`, entry point, and test project before replacing scaffold content. For existing work, repair in place and do not force re-scaffold over non-empty project directories. If a scaffold command returns an unsuccessful result, treat it as a failed attempt, inspect the result, and correct the template or path before retrying; do not assume a failed scaffold created a usable project.

For greenfield scaffold replacement, budget the tool loop around product mutation. Use one bounded file listing, inspect only the project/import/entry files and direct mutation targets, and do not read every stock template page before the first write. When several related product files must change, prefer a bounded current-run PowerShell helper executed through `workspace_pwsh_run_script` with the grounded product alias as `workingDirectory` and a `ProductMutation` side-effect manifest restricted to that alias. Inside the helper, `(Get-Location).Path` is the product root; join only product-root-relative child paths and never append the `external-target/...` alias to the current directory. If a helper invocation fails and you correct the helper, verify and invoke the corrected version again in the same execution; a helper rewrite is not a successful product mutation receipt. Then read back representative changed production and test files. Never write the final managed artifact while the product remains read-only.

Workspace command timeout arguments are seconds, not milliseconds. Prefer the tool defaults unless there is a concrete need for a longer run. For generated app tests, use `300` seconds or less unless a concrete diagnostic proves the tests need more time.

Keep domain and application logic strongly typed and testable. Put non-trivial behavior in public classes under a clear domain or application namespace, then reference the host or support library from a separate test project under the grounded product root with a `ProjectReference`. Avoid root namespace/type collisions, weakly typed state, hidden lifecycle side effects, and silent fallback paths that hide real failures.

When the requested deliverable is an app with a user-facing surface, implement a real surface for the requested topic. Do not stop with only a support library, tests, markdown notes, or an untouched template host. Replace placeholder routes, starter copy, and stock navigation with a topic-specific workflow, then prove the running app through the relevant runtime or browser tools. For greenfield user-facing apps, remove or replace stock visible scaffold chrome such as `Counter`, `Weather`, `About`, default sidebar links, starter home copy, and placeholder sample data unless the current request explicitly asks to keep them. Browser screenshots, snapshots, console logs, and state outputs must be current-run evidence, not chat-only claims or stale prior-run files, and at least one UI proof artifact must show a meaningful filled, selected, or changed state for the primary workflow. If browser tools return provider-native filenames before managed artifact import, cite those filenames; do not fail or escalate solely because workspace file tools cannot see the managed browser folder during the same attempt. For project-structure handoff, do not create a node per validation command or screenshot attempt; use the final accepted screenshot ImageAsset, one run-app proof node, one run-tests proof node, and one manager summary node, with detailed logs left under managed artifacts.

When the project structure includes a source visual target ImageAsset, treat it as implementation input. Inspect or resolve its media path when available, derive the visible composition and interaction state it implies, and make the primary route materially align with that target within the requested scope. If you cannot access or analyze the image with the assigned tools, record that blocker instead of building from memory.

For web, Blazor, or static-hosted app delivery, inspect the entry document after final source mutations and make every local `href` and `src` resolve to a real product-root asset or generated framework asset. Do not leave stale links to `css/app.css`, Bootstrap, icons, manifests, service workers, generated styles, or scripts when those files do not exist at the referenced path. If a scaffolded or generated app writes `wwwroot/app.css`, either reference `app.css` or move it to `wwwroot/css/app.css`. Browser console 404s for local product assets are validation failures, not harmless noise. For user-facing web surfaces, custom route/component class names must be backed by a loaded stylesheet or scoped component stylesheet; a page with domain-specific classes but only stock template CSS is a product defect.

For Blazor WebAssembly delivery, verify the complete runtime dependency graph from actual component and service injection sites through transitive dependencies. Register the intended abstractions, implementations, and lifetimes in the WebAssembly host, and base any repair on the current compiler, host, or post-start browser diagnostic rather than a remembered service recipe. Inspect the entry document and JavaScript loading model when current evidence points to an interop or bootstrap failure. A page that remains on the loading placeholder, renders blank, or has no enabled visible controls after current startup is a product defect even when build, test, and HTTP startup smoke pass. Validate service-worker registration, installation, update, cache, offline, or other PWA behavior only when the resolved delivery contract requires that capability.

Preserve the template-selected `TargetFramework` unless a concrete build or SDK error proves it cannot be used in the current environment. Do not downgrade or retarget projects to a remembered default framework. If a retarget is genuinely required, update every related project consistently, remove or replace APIs that are unavailable on the new framework, rerun restore/build/test, and run the host again when the deliverable is runnable.

Use the test framework selected by the resolved contract or existing test project. For greenfield work with no declared framework, choose one supported current SDK template once and keep it consistent. Do not combine runners, manually convert a scaffolded test project without diagnostic cause, invent package versions, or upgrade from memory. Preserve generated or centrally managed packages unless restore output proves a change is required. Diagnose compiler and analyzer messages against the actual framework and package version, then apply the supported framework-specific repair shown by that evidence. Prefer `ProjectReference` for declared project relationships, and do not use broad source globs as a substitute for a clean project boundary.

Do not add XML documentation comments unless the user explicitly asks for them or the existing project already uses that convention. Keep comments rare and focused on non-obvious behavior.

Validation is part of implementation. After source changes, run the narrowest relevant `workspace_dotnet_restore`, `workspace_dotnet_build`, and `workspace_dotnet_test` sequence. The .NET restore/build/test tools may target explicit `.csproj`, `.sln`, or `.slnx` files; they also accept an unambiguous project directory, but pass an explicit file when a directory contains multiple candidate projects. For generated or greenfield test projects, keep tests deterministic and bounded: do not write `while` loops that depend only on mutable app/UI state without a maximum iteration guard and an assertion that each state transition succeeded. Build, test, and analyzer warnings in generated deliverables are validation defects, not ignorable risks; if a warning cites an editable product or test file, edit that file and rerun the same command until the warning is gone before finalizing. Use a `workspace_dotnet_test` timeout of 300 seconds or less unless a real diagnostic proves the generated app tests need more time. For runnable console or worker-style projects, use `workspace_dotnet_run` with `waitForHttp: false` when a runtime smoke is required. For ASP.NET Core, web API, or Blazor apps, build first, then use `workspace_dotnet_run` with loopback HTTP startup proof. `workspace_dotnet_run` targetPath must be a runnable project file; prefer `DotNetAppProjectFileAlias` and then `DotNetAppProjectFile`, and never pass a `.sln`, `.slnx`, product root, app project directory, or other directory as the run target. Leave `keepAlive` false for startup proof that does not need same-step browser follow-up. If the same step must run Playwright/browser checks, set `keepAlive: true` with `lifetimeScope: ExecutionRun`, capture screenshot `.png`, browser_snapshot `.yml` or browser_evaluate `.json`/`.txt`/`.md` state output, and browser_console_messages `.log` as current-run evidence, then call `workspace_dotnet_stop` with the recorded `startup.json` receipt before finalizing and cite its `cleanup.json` proof. If `workspace_analyze_image` is available, use it on accepted or rejected screenshot files and cite the provider/model/token result for visual claims; if the assigned provider/model is not vision-capable, block that visual-analysis gap instead of accepting screenshot metadata alone. For time-dependent, animated, queued, asynchronous, or continuously progressing UI behavior, capture before/after state over elapsed time and prove the observable state changed as expected; if the product wording or acceptance criteria imply automatic progression, manual input proof is not a substitute. A single static screenshot is insufficient. Use `lifetimeScope: ProcessRun` only when the process graph has separate later capture and cleanup steps that consume the startup receipt.

When launch variables provide `DotNetSolutionFileAlias`, `DotNetAppProjectFileAlias`, or `DotNetTestProjectFileAlias`, use those exact grounded files before probing for alternatives. A missing guessed root-level `<App>.csproj` is not a blocker when the supplied app-project alias resolves under `src/` or another declared layout. Inspect that declared location and continue the validation yourself. Do not ask a manager to assign another agent merely because this step has not executed its required receipts yet; if the validation tools are attached, the current validation role owns calling them.

If `workspace_dotnet_restore`, `workspace_dotnet_build`, `workspace_dotnet_test`, or `workspace_dotnet_run` fails, read the returned stdout/stderr previews and any referenced `stdout.txt`, `stderr.txt`, request, or receipt artifacts before editing. Do not repeatedly rewrite `.csproj` files, retarget frameworks, add packages, change test runners, or rerun the same command from exit code alone. Diagnose the concrete compiler, restore, test, startup, or route error first, make the smallest targeted fix, then rerun the same failing command. If stdout/stderr are truncated, read the artifact paths supplied by the tool before repairing.

Final product-validation order: finish the last product source/content/configuration mutation first, then rerun every required validation that could be affected, then read at least one representative changed product file, then write durable evidence artifacts, then submit the governed step outcome. Do not mutate product files after that final read. Evidence artifacts under managed `artifacts/`, `output/`, `data/`, or `integration-map/` roots are proof records, not a reason to repeat product validation unless they are the requested product deliverable.

Before final evidence artifacts or a governed outcome, read at least one representative changed product file after the final product mutation. For app work, prefer the changed `.csproj`, entry point, routed page, domain/application class, or test source that best proves the delivered behavior. If you change another product file after that read, repeat the read and rerun the required build, test, run, browser, or deliverable validation before concluding.

If a command fails, inspect stdout, stderr, receipts, and the concrete project files before retrying. Do not repeat the same failed command until you change the cause or gather new diagnostics. Do not claim completion with only markdown evidence when source, build, test, run, browser, or artifact proof was required.

When writing xUnit tests, include a visible `using Xunit;` or project-level global using before using xUnit attributes or assertions.

Never make validation pass by writing fake package, framework, runtime, browser, or test-tool shims. Do not define local `Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting`, `Xunit`, `NUnit.Framework`, browser API, or ASP.NET Core replacement namespaces/classes to satisfy compilation. Fix the real package restore, project references, test framework choice, target framework, or environment issue; if that is impossible with available tools, return a concrete blocker instead of hiding it.

11. Before finalizing, drop any bullet that could apply to many unrelated repositories without changing the file names, type names, or method names.
12. Return 2 to 4 findings. Fewer grounded findings are better than a longer generic list.

14. If you do not have enough evidence yet, continue reading instead of presenting a generic architecture complaint as fact.

{"skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"blazor-ssr-delivery","description":"Reusable workflow guidance for creating, repairing, running, and validating Blazor Web App and component-driven ASP.NET Core UI deliverables.","instructions":"Use this skill only for Blazor app delivery and component-driven ASP.NET Core UI work, as a Blazor specialization of the concrete deliverable delivery skill. It is generic across app domains and must not inject sample topics, old output paths, or prior-run acceptance criteria. Create, repair, run, and validate Blazor Web App, Blazor SSR, interactive server, and component-library UI deliverables with maintainable, strongly typed C# plus small JavaScript interop only when the requested interaction genuinely needs browser APIs. Start with the real scaffolded project files, especially the solution file, `.csproj`, `Program.cs`, routed page, and test project, before making substantial edits.

Use existing repository conventions and the shared component library where available. Preserve the scaffolded target framework, Blazor SSR hosting shape, and chosen test framework unless the approved scope explicitly changes them. Prefer predictable component state and explicit service boundaries over hidden lifecycle side effects. Do not introduce unnecessary JavaScript, fallback mechanisms that hide failures, or speculative abstractions.

If the project structure or attached step materials name a concrete output directory, treat that directory as the real application root. When it is outside the managed workspace, use the mapped alias `external-target/<drive>/...` with workspace file and dotnet tools; do not scaffold a parallel copy under `artifacts/...`, `output/...`, or another generated implementation folder. If it already contains a `.csproj`, `.sln`, or `.slnx`, inspect and repair it in place instead of calling `workspace_dotnet_new`. Treat durable artifact paths as proof destinations only, not as substitute Blazor project roots.

When the current run names an exact generated product root, the runnable host belongs directly in that root. Do not create a scenario-named sibling app, a sibling `*.Tests` project, or a copied/probe scaffold anywhere in the process-run output tree and then treat that as the deliverable. Tests belong under `<ProductRoot>/tests/<Host>.Tests`. Do not set `BaseOutputPath`, `BaseIntermediateOutputPath`, or `MSBuildProjectExtensionsPath` in the generated host as a path-shortening workaround; use the normal `bin`/`obj` layout and the current-run workspace aliases supplied by the tools.

Keep the current brief and project structure authoritative. Do not copy old prior-example domains, remembered external target paths, or prior-run acceptance criteria into a new Blazor task unless the current run explicitly asks for them. If policy denies an external-target path, treat that denied path as stale or ungrounded for this run; switch to the current grounded product root or current-run artifacts and do not retry that path. Never inspect, cite, copy, or infer implementation patterns from sibling external-target applications on the same host. The scaffold parent directory is only a `workspace_dotnet_new` argument; it is not a product root, source corpus, evidence source, or permission to read sibling folders. Framework patterns must come from loaded skills, official templates, BaseLib/component-library resources, tool descriptions, or current-run artifacts. Do not claim contextual examples, source files, templates, or implementation references were reviewed unless this execution actually inspected them through current-run tools or loaded them from attached skill/template resources.

For greenfield modern Blazor Web App work, scaffold with `workspace_dotnet_new` template `blazor`. Architecture notes that say "Blazor Server" for a new app are shorthand for the current Blazor Web App SSR/server-interactive model and never authorize the obsolete `blazorserver` template. If a template call returns an unsuccessful result, inspect that result, switch to the approved current template, and inspect the actual generated project before editing.

Workspace command timeout arguments are seconds, not milliseconds. Prefer the tool defaults for scaffold, build, test, and run operations unless diagnostics show a real timeout. For generated app tests, use `300` seconds or less unless a concrete diagnostic proves the tests need more time.

Avoid same-name collisions between Razor components and domain types. If the domain already defines a service, model, value object, or enum whose simple name matches the UI surface you plan to add, do not create components that rely on ambiguous type resolution. Rename the UI surface or qualify the domain type explicitly so the generated build stays deterministic.

Do not bind Blazor inputs or selects to `object`, `dynamic`, or other weakly typed holders that depend on runtime conversion. Keep form state concrete and explicit so route rendering fails at compile time instead of throwing `TypeConverter` or ambiguous binding errors at runtime.

Choose one test runner before the first test-project scaffold and keep that runner for the test project. Do not scaffold the same test-project root with a second template, and do not manually convert a generated test `.csproj` from one runner to another in the same attempt. When the scaffolded tests come from `dotnet new mstest` or the generated project references the `MSTest` meta-package, respect that API surface. When writing xUnit tests, include a visible `using Xunit;` or a project-level global using before using `[Fact]`, `[Theory]`, `Assert`, or other xUnit APIs. Use the modern assertion methods exposed by the generated package, such as `Assert.Throws<T>`, `Assert.ThrowsExactly<T>`, or `Assert.HasCount(expected, collection)` when present, and avoid injecting legacy `[ExpectedException]`, `Assert.ThrowsException(...)`, or count assertions such as `Assert.AreEqual(expected, collection.Count)` when analyzer-approved alternatives exist. Preserve generated test package references and versions unless restore diagnostics explicitly prove they are unavailable. Do not replace generated MSTest references with xUnit/NUnit, or replace generated xUnit/NUnit references with MSTest, as a repair shortcut. Do not invent package versions such as a remembered latest; if restore reports `NU1102`, use the nearest version or generated template version shown by diagnostics, or return a blocker when no valid version is known.

Keep automated test projects inside the grounded product root but outside the Blazor host source folders, and make sure the host project does not include test sources, test output, or static web asset files. For a product root at `<ProductRoot>` with a host at `<ProductRoot>/<Host>.csproj` or `<ProductRoot>/src/<Host>/<Host>.csproj`, use a child such as `<ProductRoot>/tests/<Host>.Tests/<Host>.Tests.csproj`; do not create an ungrounded sibling beside `<ProductRoot>`. For `workspace_dotnet_new`, scaffold that test project with `parentDirectory: <ProductRoot>/tests` and `name: <Host>.Tests`; do not reuse the host scaffold parent directory with `name: <Host>.Tests`. If the Blazor host `.csproj` sits directly at `<ProductRoot>` and a child `tests/` or `Tests/` folder exists, inspect the host `.csproj` before final validation and add a durable exclusion unless one already exists. Prefer `<DefaultItemExcludes>$(DefaultItemExcludes);tests/**;Tests/**</DefaultItemExcludes>` in a host `PropertyGroup`; use equivalent explicit `Compile`, `Content`, `None`, and `EmbeddedResource` `Remove` entries only when that matches the project style. Do not write JSON/C#-escaped globs such as `Tests\\**\\*.cs` into `.csproj` XML. If a host build reports missing `Xunit`, `Fact`, `MSTest`, or test attribute namespaces, inspect for misplaced or included test files inside the host and move, delete, or exclude only those test sources; do not add test packages to the production host. If build or test output shows repeated nested paths such as `tests/<TestProject>/bin/.../tests/<TestProject>/bin/...`, `MSB3030` copy failures, missing `.staticwebassets.runtime.json`, missing `.staticwebassets.endpoints.json`, missing test `runtimeconfig.json`, or missing `project.assets.json` from nested test output, treat it as the Blazor host including child test output/static web assets. Repair the host layout or exclusions before rerunning. Do not recreate test files under the host after deleting them. After any test-layout or default-item repair, rerun the same host build that failed, the relevant test project, and `workspace_dotnet_run` for the runnable Blazor host.

Keep support code inside the same grounded product root. For small Blazor SSR apps, prefer `Domain/` or `Application/` folders in the host project. If the app needs a separate class library, create it below the product root, such as `<ProductRoot>/src/<Host>.Domain/<Host>.Domain.csproj`, by using a parent directory under `<ProductRoot>`. Do not scaffold `<ProductParent>/<Host>.Domain` as a sibling beside the product root unless that sibling path is explicitly grounded.

Do not rerun `workspace_dotnet_new --force` over a non-empty Blazor host or test project. Inspect and repair the existing scaffold in place; forced re-scaffolding can erase the implemented `Components/Pages` route and restore stock template content.

After `workspace_dotnet_new`, inspect the actual generated project path before assuming where the host lives. When the project structure provides an exact product root, scaffold by passing its parent as `parentDirectory` and its leaf folder as `name`, so the host is created inside that product root. Target the real scaffolded project path, and create tests under the grounded product root, typically in `tests/<Host>.Tests`.

{"skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"git-standard-operations","description":"Workflow guidance for the shipped local git workspace tools.","instructions":"# Git Standard Operations

- `workspace_git_status` inspects current change state.
- `workspace_git_diff` inspects unstaged content changes.

7. Keep branch names short, task-scoped, and readable.

- Use only the tools listed in this skill.
- Do not invent git commands or shell equivalents.

{"skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"hr-agent-capability-curation","description":"Create and validate the least-privilege reusable capabilities required by a new or managed technical agent.","instructions":"# HR agent capability curation

Use this workflow only as the exact managed HR Agent when a technical agent needs a reusable skill, tool, or MCP server that is not already available.

Search the capability catalog first with `capability_curator_catalog_search`. Reuse a suitable capability when one exists. For an exact existence check, choose the planned canonical key first and pass that exact key as the entire `text` value. The search text is a literal substring, so never concatenate keywords such as `"garden gardening vegetable herb"` for this check. Search the exact display name separately only when needed.

Repeat that exact-key search after every approval continuation, rejected approval, resumed run, or new user turn. If exactly one capability with the planned key already exists, the save stage is complete: do not draft or invoke another `capability_curator_save`. Retain its capability ID and fingerprint, inspect it with `capability_curator_editor_get`, and continue from the persisted result. If none exists, draft the smallest typed save candidate from the `capability_curator_save` schema, describe it, and request explicit approval before saving it.

Create focused reusable knowledge as an inline Skill with `capability_curator_save`. Set `SkillConfiguration.InlineName` to a technical lowercase kebab-case identifier such as `garden-planning-knowledge`; use the separate capability `Name` for the human-readable title. Keep instructions factual, bounded to the requested domain, and explicit about assumptions, validation, and safety constraints. Do not hide broad authority or unrelated workflows in a skill.

For a Tool or MCP server, use typed configuration only. Never put credentials or secret values in capability configuration; use approved secret bindings. Run the matching setup test first, then pass its one-time attestation to `capability_curator_save`. A failed, stale, or mismatched attestation is a stop condition. The setup test and save remain separate host approvals within the same capability-authoring stage; do not insert an unrelated mutation between them or reuse the one-time attestation for another candidate.

After a capability is saved, create the requested agent as Draft with `hr_agent_create` and include the new capability ID in its least-privilege capability set. After a capability save succeeds, read it back with `capability_curator_editor_get`, report its ID and fingerprint, then stop and ask the user to continue with agent creation. After agent creation or update succeeds, read the agent back, report its ID, settings, and assigned capability ID, then stop and ask the user to continue with assignment verification. Do not create or assign a capability merely to grant these tools. On creation, omitted nested fields default to no grant. On update, this object is a nested patch: omitted booleans and project IDs preserve their current values, so send only the smallest changed field set. capabilities.configurationJson:
{"skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"spreadsheet","description":"Guidance and assets for creating, reading, and analyzing spreadsheet content.","instructions":"# Spreadsheet Internal Agent Skill

Use this skill when an internal agent reads, validates, or produces spreadsheet-like artifacts.

Work rules:

- Inspect workbook structure before summarizing or editing.
- Preserve tab names, headers, formulas, and data types unless the step explicitly asks for changes.
- For generated spreadsheets, validate the workbook can be opened or inspected and that expected sheets and key cells exist.
- Keep reconciliation outputs explicit about matched records, unmatched records, and uncertainty.
- Do not claim spreadsheet proof from a text-only summary.

Workbook workflow:

- Use `workspace_inspect_spreadsheet` for a compact preview of incoming `.xls`, `.xlsx`, `.csv`, or `.tsv` files.
- Use `workspace_spreadsheet_summary` for `.xlsx` workbook sheet names, positions, used ranges, and dimensions before editing.
- Use `workspace_read_spreadsheet_range` for tables and `workspace_read_spreadsheet_cell` for exact key cells.
- Use `workspace_write_spreadsheet` to create or update `.xlsx` workbooks. Put values in `cellWrites` for individual cells and `rangeWrites` for rectangular tables.
- For every `rangeWrites` item, the outer `values` count must fit within the rows of `rangeAddress`, and every inner row must fit within its columns. Use empty rows with the same column count as the table, or omit unused trailing cells.
- If a spreadsheet tool returns a retryable input failure, correct the reported address, row, or column mismatch and retry. A retryable result means the tool is available; do not report spreadsheet creation as unsupported.
- Use one logical worksheet per concern: source data, assumptions, calculations, and summary. Keep sheet names short and stable, for example `Quotation`, `Assumptions`, `Margin`, and `Summary`.
- After writing, inspect the workbook and read back representative cells or ranges. Do not report success until the workbook exists and the expected sheets, headers, and formulas are visible.

Formula rules:

- Values beginning with `=` are stored as Excel-compatible A1 formulas by `workspace_write_spreadsheet`.
- Use `workspace_spreadsheet_function_catalog` when building formulas. It returns common function names, syntax, examples, and notes.
- Keep formulas readable and auditable. Prefer helper columns over deeply nested formulas.
- Use `IFERROR` around ratios that can divide by zero, such as margin formulas.
- Use absolute references like `$B$2` only when a formula will be copied and the referenced cell must not move.
- Store uncertain or user-supplied assumptions on an assumptions sheet and reference those cells from calculations.

Common formula patterns:

- Total: `=SUM(D2:D20)`
- Gross profit: `=Revenue-Cost`
- Gross margin: `=IFERROR((Revenue-Cost)/Revenue,"")`
- Conditional total: `=SUMIFS(D2:D20,A2:A20,"Hardware")`
- Lookup price: `=XLOOKUP(A2,Items!A:A,Items!D:D,"Missing")`
- Scenario label: `=IFS(E2>=0.4,"High",E2>=0.25,"Medium",TRUE,"Low")`

When converting a PDF, DOCX, or other document into a workbook:

- Use `workspace_convert_document` first and extract source facts from the returned markdown/output path.
- Keep source facts separate from calculations. Put extracted quotation rows on a source-data sheet and formulas on a calculation sheet.
- Include the source path, extraction assumptions, currency, units, and missing-data notes in the workbook.

Use assigned document/spreadsheet workspace tools when available.

capabilities.configurationJson:
{"skillSource":"inline","inlineSkill":{"name":"svg-authoring","description":"Author and verify well-formed, safe SVG XML before registering project assets or rasterizing layouts.","instructions":"# SVG authoring

Use this skill whenever the requested deliverable includes an SVG file or an SVG-backed project asset.

## Authoring contract

- Treat SVG as XML, not as tolerant HTML. Use one balanced `<svg>` document root with `xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"`, quote every attribute, close every element, and keep IDs unique.
- Escape all dynamic text and labels before placing them in XML. In text and attribute values, write `&` as `&` and `<` as `<`; escape `>` as `>` when it could close markup. In attributes, also escape the quote character used to delimit that attribute.
- Prefer SVG-native shapes, paths, text, groups, transforms, and styles. Do not add scripts, event-handler attributes, external resource references, or `foreignObject` content.
- Check every `url(#id)`, `href="#id"`, clip path, mask, marker, gradient, and filter reference against a declared unique ID.
- Keep each requested variant in its own file unless the user explicitly asks for a combined sheet.

## Required verification

1. Review the complete serialized SVG for raw ampersands, unbalanced tags, unquoted attributes, duplicate IDs, and broken ID references before registering it.
2. Create the project asset with `project_structure_asset_create`. The platform parses SVG XML and returns an actionable line and position when the document is malformed. Correct the source file and retry; do not bypass or relabel invalid SVG as another content type.
3. Read the created asset and its content back with `project_structure_asset_get` and `project_structure_asset_content_get`. Do not claim an SVG deliverable is complete until both the write and readback succeed.
4. If a raster rendition is requested, use the image-generation tool with an explicitly configured image provider. Store the resulting PNG or WebP as a separate asset; never claim that an image was generated when the tool failed or no binary file was produced.
